title: Objectwise comparison of cone straightening with the slice-pullback diagram
statement:
Use the marked simplicial sets, absolute model $\mathsf M$ and relative (co)cartesian models of [lem-coef-marked-point-cartesian-model] and [lem-coef-marked-relative-cartesian-model], projective diagrams of [lem-coef-simplicial-projective-model-calculus], and coherent realization and marked cone straightening of [lem-coef-coherent-nerve-comparison] and [lem-coef-marked-cone-straightening-quillen]. Work in nested universes large enough for the following small constructions. For a small ordinary category $C$ and any marked simplicial set $p:X\to N(C)$, define a strict diagram $L_C(X):C\to\mathsf M$ by
$$L_C(X)(c)_r=\{(x,g):x\in X_r,\quad g:p(x_r)\to c\text{ in }C\}.$$
Here $p(x_r)$ is the image of the last vertex of $x$, and $p(x_i\to x_j)$ is the corresponding arrow in the string $p(x)$. For $\theta:[s]\to[r]$ set
$$\theta^*(x,g)=(\theta^*x,\ g\circ p(x_{\theta(s)}\to x_r)).$$
An edge $(e,g)$ is marked exactly when $e$ is marked in $X$; the action of $c\to d$ postcomposes $g$. Equivalently the underlying simplicial set is $X\times_{N(C)}N(C_{/c})$, where $C_{/c}$ has objects arrows to $c$ and morphisms their commuting triangles. Let
$$\epsilon_C:\mathfrak C[N(C)^{\mathrm{op}}]\to C^{\mathrm{op}},\qquad T_C(X)=\bigl(\operatorname{St}^+_{\epsilon_C}(X^{\mathrm{op}})\bigr)^{\mathrm{op}},$$
where $C^{\mathrm{op}}$ has discrete mapping simplicial sets and the final opposite is taken separately at every value of the $C$-diagram. Opposite of a marked simplicial set reverses vertex order and carries its marked edges to the reversed marked edges.

There is a natural transformation $a_C:T_C\to L_C$ such that for every $X$ and every $c\in C$, the map $a_{C,X}(c)$ is a weak equivalence in $\mathsf M$. No fibrancy or cofibrancy assumption on $X$ is required. For the terminal category $C=*$, the transformation $a_*$ is the natural point comparison $T_*\to\mathrm{id}$ obtained from the cone-straightening point comparison.

The transformation is natural in both $X$ and $C$: for $u:C\to D$, write $N(u)_!X$ for $X$ with base map composed with $N(u)$, and let $u_!$ denote ordinary left Kan extension of marked diagrams, characterized by $\operatorname{Nat}(u_!H,G)=\operatorname{Nat}(H,Gu)$. Under the canonical cone and slice-diagram identifications
$$u_!T_C(X)\cong T_D(N(u)_!X),\qquad u_!L_C(X)\cong L_D(N(u)_!X),$$
$u_!a_{C,X}$ agrees with $a_{D,N(u)_!X}$. These identifications and this equality respect identities and composites.

source.place: HTT Remarks 3.2.5.10 and 3.2.5.16, Lemma 3.2.5.17(2), and the point normalization of Proposition 3.2.1.14. Read online; no Stacks tag states this marked-simplicial comparison. WANTED: local archive of HTT.

proof.text: First fix the variance. Write $Y=X^{\mathrm{op}}$, and let $P_X=C^{\mathrm{op}}\amalg_{\mathfrak C[Y]}\mathfrak C[Y\star\Delta^0]$. Then $T_C(X)(c)=P_X(c,*)^{\mathrm{op}}$, including its marking; the last opposite must not be omitted. The ordinary nerve and coherent nerve of the discrete simplicial category $C^{\mathrm{op}}$ agree, so the coherent-realization counit supplies the required base functor. For $L_C$, the formula in the statement satisfies $(\theta\eta)^*=\eta^*\theta^*$ because the two last-vertex arrows compose; postcomposition in $c$ commutes with these operators. Thus its displayed pairs and markings define an actual strict diagram, identified with the marked slice pullback.

Construct the comparison before proving it is an equivalence. Define a simplicial category $B_X$ with objects those of $C^{\mathrm{op}}$ and a new object $*$, old mapping sets those of $C^{\mathrm{op}}$, $B_X(c,*)=L_C(X)(c)^{\mathrm{op}}$, $B_X(*,c)=\varnothing$, and $B_X(*,*)=\Delta^0$. Its old-to-cone composition is the opposite of postcomposition on the label of $L_C$. Here is a functor $\mathfrak C[Y\star\Delta^0]\to B_X$ extending the base functor on $\mathfrak C[Y]$. On a simplex $y:\Delta^n\to Y$, the coherent mapping set from $a$ to the new cone vertex is the nerve of subsets of $\{a,\ldots,n,*\}$ containing $a,*$. On an $r$-simplex $I_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq I_r$ put $m_k=\max(I_k\setminus\{*\})$. Send it to the simplex of $L_C(X)(p(y_a))^{\mathrm{op}}$ represented by $y|_{m_0,\ldots,m_r}$ and by the arrow $p(y_a\to y_{m_0})$ in $C^{\mathrm{op}}$ (equivalently its reversed arrow in $C$). Deleting or repeating an $I_k$ gives exactly the simplicial operators of $L_C^{\mathrm{op}}$. A monotone map of the base simplex commutes with the maximum of a nonempty finite subset, so these formulas agree on faces and degeneracies. Composition of a coherent old-to-old path with an old-to-cone path takes the union of subsets; its maximum is the maximum from the latter path, and its arrow label is the composite base arrow. This checks composition and also shows that the map on old mapping objects factors through the counit to $C^{\mathrm{op}}$. The pushout property therefore induces $P_X(c,*)\to L_C(X)(c)^{\mathrm{op}}$. On the distinguished cone edge of a marked edge of $Y$ the image has that same underlying edge, reversed back in $X$; its image in $L_C$ is marked. Precomposition only changes the arrow label and preserves this marking. Taking opposites gives a marked map $a_{C,X}(c)$, natural in $c$ and in marked maps $X\to X'$.

source.place: Remark 3.2.5.10, existence construction; Remark 3.2.5.16. Explicit coherent-subset formula supplied here.

proof.text: Opposite is an equivalence of the category of marked simplicial sets and preserves its absolute weak equivalences: there is an identity $\operatorname{Map}^{\sharp}(A^{\mathrm{op}},K^\natural)=\operatorname{Map}^{\sharp}(A,(K^{\mathrm{op}})^\natural)^{\mathrm{op}}$, obtained by reversing both factors in the defining product. Reversal of barycentric coordinates identifies the realizations of a simplicial set and its opposite. Since $K\mapsto K^{\mathrm{op}}$ permutes test quasicategories, the weak-equivalence tests are unchanged. Monomorphisms are unchanged too, so the lifting characterization of fibrations shows that opposite preserves trivial fibrations. Applied valuewise it permutes objectwise trivial fibrations; reversing a lifting square then proves preservation of projective cofibrations.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.1.4; Proposition 3.2.1.7; Lemma 3.2.5.15; explicit free boundary and marking attachments.

proof.text: Both functors preserve small colimits. For $T_C$ use the cone-straightening adjunction and the opposite equivalence of step 3. For $L_C$ compute colimits degreewise: the fiber of pairs over a simplex is its set of outgoing arrow labels, and markings in a colimit are precisely those generated by the images of marked edges. They also send monomorphisms to objectwise cofibrations. For $L_C$ the map on pairs is injective. For $T_C$ use the cone left-Quillen property, relative monomorphism cofibrations, evaluation preserving projective cofibrations, and step 3.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.1.4; Proposition 3.2.1.7; Lemma 3.2.5.15; explicit free boundary and marking attachments.

proof.text: The free boundary and marking-cell lemma gives projective cofibrancy of every $L_C(X)$ by its stated monomorphism clause applied to $\varnothing\to X$. Every $T_C(X)$ is projectively cofibrant because all relative marked objects are cofibrant, cone straightening is left Quillen, and valuewise opposite preserves projective cofibrations by step 3.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.1.4; Proposition 3.2.1.7; Lemma 3.2.5.15; explicit free boundary and marking attachments.

proof.text: For $u:C\to D$, cone substitution and the opposite equivalence give $u_!T_C(X)\cong T_D(N(u)_!X)$. For the slice side, a degree-$r$ representative of its left Kan colimit at $d$ is $(h:u(c)\to d,x,g:p(x_r)\to c)$, with relation $(h\circ u(k),x,g)\sim(h,x,k\circ g)$. This quotient computes the left Kan extension: a map out is exactly a family of maps $L_C(X)(c)\to G(u(c))$ compatible with the $C$-action, by composing with $G(h)$. Send a representative to $(x,h\circ u(g))$; its inverse takes $(x,l)$ to $c=p(x_r),g=1,h=l$. The relation with $k=g$ proves the inverse identities. The last-face label on both sides is $h\circ u(g)\circ u(p(x_{r-1}\to x_r))$; all other faces and degeneracies restrict $x$, and actions postcompose $h$. Markings depend only on the $X$-edge, so this is an isomorphism of marked diagrams. All indexing sets and comma categories are small.

source.place: Remarks 3.2.5.8, 3.2.5.10(1)-(2), 3.2.5.14 and 3.2.5.16; point normalization in Section 3.2.1.

proof.text: The underlying comparison in step 2 is the normalized unmarked comparison: on $[n]$, reversing the order changes the displayed maximum-of-subsets rule to its minimum-of-subsets rule, and the same cone quotient relations are imposed. The cited unmarked statement gives its compatibility with base change, identities and composites. Step 6 lifts the underlying Kan identifications to marked identifications. Since marked maps are determined by their underlying maps, this proves $u_!a_{C,X}=a_{D,N(u)_!X}$ with the same coherence. Equivalently the representative formula changes only the arrow label by $g\mapsto h\circ u(g)$, and iterated substitution is associative.

source.place: Remarks 3.2.5.8, 3.2.5.10(1)-(2), 3.2.5.14 and 3.2.5.16; point normalization in Section 3.2.1.

proof.text: Over the terminal category the underlying cone-straightening functor is the coend $T^0(X)=\int^{[n]}X_n\times Q^n$ of the generator-calculation node. The uniqueness lemma identifies the restriction to all minimally marked simplices of any natural point comparison $T^0\to\mathrm{id}$ with the maximum augmentation. The coend coprojections therefore identify it on every minimally marked object; naturality for $X^\flat\to X$, whose underlying map is the identity, identifies it for arbitrary markings as well. A marked map is determined by its underlying map. Applying the two opposite operations and their canonical double-opposite identification gives exactly the stipulated comparison for $T_*$.

source.place: Remarks 3.2.5.8, 3.2.5.10(1)-(2), 3.2.5.14 and 3.2.5.16; point normalization in Section 3.2.1.

proof.text: Call $X\to N(C)$ good when every $a_{C,X}(c)$ is a weak equivalence in the absolute marked model. The empty object is good. The class is closed under small coproducts and under a pushout of good objects when one leg is a monomorphism: apply both colimit-preserving functors and evaluate at $c$, use step 4 to obtain cofibration legs, and use the coproduct and span comparison clauses for cofibrant objects. It is also closed under small continuous transfinite unions by the transfinite comparison clause. Every object in the absolute marked model is cofibrant, so the comparison lemmas' cofibrancy hypotheses hold at each stage. This uses only coproducts, cofibration pushouts and continuous ordinal colimits, never an arbitrary colimit of weak equivalences.

source.place: Lemma 3.2.5.17(2), proof (A)-(B), in its cofibrant cellular form.

proof.text: Every marked simplex of dimension zero or one over $N(C)$ is good, in fact its comparison is an isomorphism. For a vertex over $b$, both values at $c$ are the discrete set $C(b,c)$. For an edge $b_0\xrightarrow{f}b_1$, both values are the simplicial graph with vertices $(0,g_0)$ and $(1,g_1)$ for $g_i:b_i\to c$, and one nondegenerate edge $(0,g_1f)\to(1,g_1)$ for each $g_1:b_1\to c$. This follows by forming the coherent realization of the coned edge: its mapping interval has the two displayed endpoints, and precomposition appends the arrow label. The map of step 2 is the identity on these vertices and edges. Such an edge is marked on both sides exactly when the input edge is marked. This covers both $(\Delta^1)^\flat$ and $(\Delta^1)^\sharp$, even when $f$ is an identity or the label set is empty.

source.place: Lemma 3.2.5.17(2), proof (C); direct dimension-zero/one cone calculation.

proof.text: For use with higher simplices, the minimally marked spine inclusion is a trivial cofibration both absolutely and over any base, and remains so after opposite. To check the exact class: the spine lemma gives the left lifting property against all underlying inner fibrations. Apply the small-object factorization to the finite-domain minimally marked inner horns. Maps right orthogonal to these horns are precisely the maps with underlying inner fibrations; the spine, with minimal markings, therefore retracts from a continuous cell composite of those horns. Finite horn domains satisfy the required smallness because a map from one uses finitely many simplices. Such a retract is marked anodyne by the marked-anodyne definition. The absolute and relative sharp-mapping restriction assertions show that it is a weak equivalence, and it is a monomorphism. Opposite exchanges the inner horns $\Lambda_i^m$ and $\Lambda_{m-i}^m$, so the same argument applies after reversal. In particular cone straightening sends the opposite spine inclusion to an objectwise weak equivalence.

source.place: Lemma 3.2.5.17(2), proof (E); inner-anodyne spine and marked relative lifting.

proof.text: Let $Z=\operatorname{Sp}[n]\subseteq\Delta^n$. First work over $N([n])=\Delta^n$ with its identity base map. The slice formula gives $L_{[n]}((\Delta^n)^\flat)(i)=(\Delta^i)^\flat$ and $L_{[n]}(Z^\flat)(i)=\operatorname{Sp}[i]^\flat$: a simplex labelled by an arrow from its last vertex to $i$ is exactly a simplex supported on $0,\ldots,i$. Thus $L_{[n]}(Z^\flat)\to L_{[n]}((\Delta^n)^\flat)$ is an objectwise weak equivalence by step 11 (and the identity for $i=0,1$). Both diagrams are projectively cofibrant by step 5. For an arbitrary simplex $\sigma:[n]\to C$, restriction $\sigma^*$ preserves projective fibrations and trivial fibrations since these are objectwise; its left adjoint $\sigma_!$ is therefore left Quillen by the lifting adjunction. The model-category preservation theorem then says it preserves weak equivalences between projectively cofibrant objects. Step 6 identifies its image with $L_C(Z^\flat)\to L_C((\Delta^n)^\flat)$ for the given base map. No assertion that an arbitrary left Kan extension preserves every objectwise equivalence is used.

source.place: Lemma 3.2.5.17(2), proof (F)-(G), with projective cofibrancy verified before Kan extension.

proof.text: Every minimally marked simplex over $N(C)$ is now good. Its spine is an iterated pushout of its consecutive edges along vertices; steps 9 and 10 show that this spine is good. The naturality square for the spine inclusion has top horizontal map $T_C(Z^\flat)(c)\to T_C((\Delta^n)^\flat)(c)$ a weak equivalence by step 11, bottom horizontal map the $L_C$ inclusion a weak equivalence by step 12, and left vertical map a weak equivalence by goodness of the spine. Two-out-of-three makes the right vertical map a weak equivalence. This proves the assertion for all $n$, with the already computed cases $n=0,1$ as bases.

Finally construct $X^\flat$ by its skeletal filtration. At stage $n$ adjoin the coproduct of its nondegenerate $n$-simplices along their boundaries. For $n=0$ these boundaries are empty; for $n>0$ each boundary is built from simplices of smaller dimension, hence is good by induction using the already established coproduct and pushout closures. All attaching simplices are good by step 13. Step 9 proves goodness at each skeletal stage and at the continuous union, so $X^\flat$ is good. Well-order the set of nondegenerate marked edges of $X$ and then adjoin each marking by the pushout of $(\Delta^1)^\flat\to(\Delta^1)^\sharp$ along that edge, always retaining the given map to $N(C)$. These are monomorphisms, their two test objects are good by step 10, and at limit stages take the continuous union. Step 9 proves that the resulting marked object $X$ is good. Degenerate edges were already marked, so this construction produces exactly $X$, including empty objects, constant base maps and arbitrary infinite markings. Combined with steps 2, 7 and 8, this proves every clause of the statement.

source.place: Lemma 3.2.5.17(2), proof (A)-(E), explicit skeletal and marking induction.

split_report.blueprint: The fourteen steps preserve the inherited route: cone comparison construction; opposite, colimit and cofibrancy calculus; explicit left-Kan calculation and normalization; good-object gluing, spine reduction and cellular induction. The two new lemmas isolate the nontrivial subarguments of the inherited steps 3 and 4; both trace through this item to thm-cbc-finite-level-proetale.

tool_uses.why: Coherent realization by subset mapping posets and the ordinary/coherent nerve identification used to construct the actual comparison.
Boundary-cell filtration of simplicial monomorphisms used for free-diagram cofibrancy and the final skeleton induction.
Minimally marked inner horns generate marked anodyne maps and their sharp restriction tests are trivial fibrations.
Identifies the terminal-base maximum-of-subsets augmentation with the stipulated point normalization.
Cone pushout, marking generators, left-Quillen property and coherent substitution; these are generic marked-model tools.
Absolute marked weak equivalences, cofibrancy and two-out-of-three.
Relative monomorphism cofibrations, cofibrancy and reversal to the cocartesian model.
Coproduct, cofibrant span and continuous ordinal comparison; no compact-support-unit statement supplies model-category gluing.
Left Quillen functors preserve weak equivalences between cofibrant objects, applied only after projective cofibrancy is proved.
The relative sharp restriction theorem proves the required relative weak equivalence of a marked spine.
Projective objectwise fibrations/weak equivalences, free diagrams and evaluation.
Converts the inner-spine lifting property to a retract of horn cells, with finite horn-domain smallness checked.

Steps 6 and 7 take its specified normalized unmarked comparison and its compatibility with left Kan extension along u, identities and composites; no node of sk-prop-sf-cbc states the unmarked relative-nerve cone comparison.
